claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Fascin limits Myosin dynamics on the migrating border cell cluster.
claims.source: These results suggest that Fascin limits Myosin dynamics on the migrating border cell cluster.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the live imaging data.

claims.claim: Increased Myosin activity increases actomyosin contractility and cell stiffness.
claims.source: As increased Myosin activity increases actomyosin contractility and cell stiffness, we next wanted to directly measure the stiffness of fascin-null follicles.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Substrate stiffness is thought to be a driving regulator of cell migration and migrating cell stiffness.
claims.source: Substrate stiffness is thought to be a driving regulator of cell migration and migrating cell stiffness (Di Martino et al., 2016; Gasparski et al., 2017; Oakes, 2018; Ren et al., 2021), therefore we aimed to directly quantify nurse cell stiffness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Martino et al., 2016; Gasparski et al., 2017; Oakes, 2018; Ren et al., 2021.

claims.claim: AFM is a standard method to directly measure mechanical properties of biological tissues.
claims.source: AFM is a standard method to directly measure mechanical properties of biological tissues (Kreplak, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kreplak, 2016.

claims.claim: AFM can be used to quantify the elastic modulus, which is a measurement of how easily an elastic material is deformed when a known amount of force is applied.
claims.source: AFM can be used to quantify the elastic modulus, which is a measurement of how easily an elastic material is deformed when a known amount of force is applied (Kreplak, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kreplak, 2016.

claims.claim: A high elastic modulus value corresponds to a stiff tissue.
claims.source: A high elastic modulus value corresponds to a stiff tissue.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about elastic modulus.

claims.claim: The nurse cells are the substrate for the border cells and their stiffness regulates border cell migration and cluster stiffness.
claims.source: The nurse cells are the substrate for the border cells and their stiffness regulates border cell migration and cluster stiffness (Aranjuez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Aranjuez et al., 2016.

claims.claim: During S9, the nurse cells are surrounded by a layer of stretch follicle cells and a basement membrane that envelopes the entire follicle.
claims.source: Notably, during S9, the nurse cells are surrounded by a layer of stretch follicle cells and a basement membrane that envelopes the entire follicle (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: There is significant difference in stiffness between the basement membrane and the underlying nurse cells in Drosophila follicles.
claims.source: Previous measurements on Drosophila follicles using AFM established that there is significant difference in stiffness between the basement membrane and the underlying nurse cells (Crest et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Crest et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Different tissue stiffnesses can be separated by using different indentation ranges to indent the AFM probe into just the basement membrane or to indent deeper into the nurse cells.
claims.source: These different tissues stiffnesses can be separated by using different indentation ranges to indent the AFM probe into just the basement membrane or to indent deeper into the nurse cells (Figure 3B; Chlasta et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chlasta et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: By using two indentation ranges to fit the mechanical response, we can quantify the distinct stiffness of the basement membrane versus that of the underlying nurse cells.
claims.source: Thus, by using two indentation ranges to fit the mechanical response, we can quantify the distinct stiffness of the basement membrane versus that of the underlying nurse cells (Chlasta et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chlasta et al., 2017.

claims.claim: For an indentation range of 0–100 nm, which probes the basement membrane, wild-type follicles have an average stiffness of 24.2 kPa and fascin-null follicles have a similar average stiffness of 26.5 kPa.
claims.source: For an indentation range of 0–100 nm, which probes the basement membrane, wild-type follicles have an average stiffness of 24.2 kPa and fascin-null follicles have a similar average stiffness of 26.5 kPa (Figure 3D, p > 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: For an indentation range of 310–550 nm, which probes the nurse cell stiffness, wild-type follicles have an average stiffness of 10.1 kPa while fascin-null follicles have a significantly increased average stiffness of 25.9 kPa.
claims.source: However, for an indentation range of 310–550 nm, which probes the nurse cell stiffness, wild-type follicles have an average stiffness of 10.1 kPa while fascin-null follicles have a significantly increased average stiffness of 25.9 kPa (Figure 3D, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 3D with p < 0.0001.

claims.claim: The stiffness of the fascin-null nurse cells is >2 x higher than wild-type nurse cells.
claims.source: Thus, the stiffness of the fascin-null nurse cells is >2 x higher than wild-type nurse cells.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the AFM measurements (25.9 kPa / 10.1 kPa).

claims.claim: Loss of Fascin increases the stiffness of the nurse cells in S9 Drosophila follicles.
claims.source: Together these results demonstrate that loss of Fascin increases the stiffness of the nurse cells in S9 Drosophila follicles.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM data.

claims.claim: Increased stiffness of the nurse cells or border cells inhibits border cell migration.
claims.source: As increased stiffness of the nurse cells or border cells inhibits border cell migration (Aranjuez et al., 2016), we hypothesized that the increased Myosin activity in fascin-null follicles contributes to the previously characterized border cell migration delays (Lamb et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Aranjuez et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Y-27632 is a Rho inhibitor previously used to reduce Myosin activity in Drosophila follicles.
claims.source: Follicles were incubated for 2 hr in either control media or 200 µM of Y-27632, a Rho inhibitor previously used to reduce Myosin activity in Drosophila follicles (He et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Y-27632 reduces activated Myosin levels on both the nurse cells and border cells.
claims.source: This inhibitor reduces activated Myosin levels on both the nurse cells and border cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: A migration index of approximately one indicates on-time migration during S9.
claims.source: A migration index of approximately one indicates on-time migration during S9, while a value less that one indicates delayed migration and a value greater than one indicates an accelerated migration.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the migration index metric.

claims.claim: A migration index value less than one indicates delayed migration.
claims.source: A migration index of approximately one indicates on-time migration during S9, while a value less that one indicates delayed migration and a value greater than one indicates an accelerated migration.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the migration index metric.

claims.claim: A migration index value greater than one indicates an accelerated migration.
claims.source: A migration index of approximately one indicates on-time migration during S9, while a value less that one indicates delayed migration and a value greater than one indicates an accelerated migration.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the migration index metric.

claims.claim: Loss of Fascin significantly delays border cell migration.
claims.source: As we previously established, loss of Fascin significant delays migration (Figure 1C, Lamb et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamb et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Inhibiting Myosin activity with Y-27632 in fascin-null follicles restores on-time border cell migration compared to the fascin-null control.
claims.source: Here, we find that inhibiting Myosin activity with Y-27632 in fascin-null follicles restores on-time border cell migration compared to the fascin-null control (Figure 4C–D and G, migration index 1.1 compared to 0.78) and is not significantly different from the wild-type control (Figure 4B and G, migration index 1.1 compared to 0.95).
claims.evidence: This is supported by migration index data shown in Figure 4C–D and G.

claims.claim: Germline knockdown of MRLC in fascin mutants significantly decreased active Myosin levels on the nurse cells compared to fascin-null controls.
claims.source: Germline knockdown of MRLC in fascin mutants significantly decreased active Myosin levels on the nurse cells compared to fascin-null controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Germline knockdown of MRLC fails to restore normal levels of active Myosin on the border cell cluster.
claims.source: However, it fails to restore normal levels of active Myosin on the border cell cluster, as Myosin activation remains significantly increased compared to the wild-type control and is not signficantly different than the fascin-null control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Germline knockdown of MRLC in fascin mutant follicles rescues border cell migration.
claims.source: Germline knockdown of MRLC in fascin mutant follicles rescues border cell migration (Figure 4E, F and H, migration index 0.91 compared to 0.65).
claims.evidence: This is supported by migration index data shown in Figure 4E, F and H.

claims.claim: Fascin is required to limit Myosin activity within the nurse cells to promote on-time border cell migration.
claims.source: Together these results suggest that Fascin is required to limit Myosin activity within the nurse cells to promote on-time border cell migration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the germline knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of Fascin at serine 52 (S52, mammalian S39) inhibits its F-actin bundling function.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of Fascin at serine 52 (S52, mammalian S39) inhibits its F-actin bundling function (Yamakita et al., 1996; Ono et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamakita et al., 1996; Ono et al., 1997.

claims.claim: If Fascin's bundling activity is required to limit Myosin activation, phosphomimetic Fascin (S52E) in fascin-null mutants would fail to suppress the increased active Myosin.
claims.source: If Fascin's bundling activity is required to limit Myosin activation, we would predict that global expression (actin 5 c GAL4) of phosphomimetic Fascin (S52E) in fascin-null mutants would fail to suppress the increased active Myosin.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis.

claims.claim: Global expression of wild-type Fascin (GFP-Fascin) in fascin mutant follicles significantly reduces active MRLC enrichment on both the nurse cell membranes and border cell cluster.

claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claims.claim: When the phosphomimetic form of Fascin (GFP-Fascin S52E) is expressed in fascin-null mutants, high levels of active Myosin are observed on both the nurse cell membranes and border cell cluster that are not significantly different than the fascin mutant control.
claims.source: Conversely, when the phosphomimetic form of Fascin (GFP-Fascin S52E) is expressed in fascin-null mutants, we observe high levels of active Myosin on both the nurse cell membranes (Figure 5C, blue arrows and D) and border cell cluster (Figure 5C, orange arrows and E) that are not significantly different than the fascin mutant control (Figure 5A, D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, D and E.

claims.claim: Fascin limits Myosin activity by bundling F-actin and precluding Myosin's ability to bind to actin filaments.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphomimetic Fascin experiments.

claims.claim: Global expression of phosphomimetic Fascin (S52E) in fascin mutant follicles only partially rescues delays in border cell migration.
claims.source: As expected, when we quantify the migration index (described in Figure 4A) for fascin mutant follicles with global expression of phosphomimetic Fascin (S52E), we find it only partially rescues delays in border cell migration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, migration index 0.90 compared to 0.80).
claims.evidence: This is supported by migration index data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Fascin functions in other ways besides bundling F-actin and limiting Myosin activity to promote on-time border cell migration.
claims.source: Together these data indicate Fascin functions in other ways besides bundling F-actin and limiting Myosin activity to promote on-time border cell migration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the partial rescue by phosphomimetic Fascin.

claims.claim: The stiffness of the nurse cells regulates border cell cluster stiffness as indicated by active Myosin levels and on-time border cell migration.
claims.source: Previous evidence demonstrated that the stiffness of the nurse cells regulates border cell cluster stiffness as indicated by active Myosin levels and on-time border cell migration (Aranjuez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Aranjuez et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Fascin is required in both the nurse cells and the border cells to promote on-time border cell migration.
claims.source: Since Fascin is required in both the nurse cells and the border cells to promote on-time border cell migration (Lamb et al., 2020), we wanted to determine which cells Fascin acts in to regulate Myosin activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamb et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Fascin in the germline results in a significant increase in pMRLC enrichment on the nurse cell membranes.
claims.source: We observe, as expected, knockdown of Fascin in the germline results in a significant increase in pMRLC (active MRLC) enrichment on the nurse cell membranes (Figure 6C, blue arrows and F, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and F with p < 0.0001.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Fascin in the germline unexpectedly fails to alter active MRLC enrichment on the border cell cluster.
claims.source: However, knockdown down of Fascin in the germline unexpectedly fails to alter active MRLC enrichment on the border cell cluster (Figure 6C, orange arrow and G, p > 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and G with p > 0.05.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Fascin in the border cells significantly increases active MRLC on the border cell cluster.
claims.source: As expected, we observe a significant increase of active MRLC on the border cell cluster when Fascin is knocked down in the border cells (Figure 6D, E and G, orange arrows, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, E and G with p < 0.0001.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Fascin in the somatic or just the border cells significantly increased active MRLC enrichment on the nurse cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, knockdown of Fascin in the somatic or just the border cells also significantly increased active MRLC enrichment on the nurse cells (Figure 6D, E and F, blue arrows, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, E and F with p < 0.0001.

results.result: Loss of Fascin increases activated Myosin on both border cells and nurse cells, decreases Myosin dynamics, and increases nurse cell stiffness, providing the first in vivo evidence that Fascin regulates Myosin activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C5 and C63-C65 provide converging experimental evidence from pMRLC immunostaining (Figure 2B-D, p<0.0001), live imaging of MRLC-GFP dynamics (Figure 2G-I, puncta lifetime increased from 70.2s to 151.8s, p<0.0001), and AFM measurements (Figure 3D, nurse cell stiffness increased from 10.1 kPa to 25.9 kPa, p<0.0001). The controls showing no change in phalloidin intensity (C68), cytoplasmic pMRLC (C69), or Myosin heavy chain levels (C70) strengthen the conclusion that the effect is specific to Myosin activation rather than protein expression changes.

results.result: Reducing Myosin activity through pharmacological inhibition or germline knockdown rescues border cell migration delays in fascin mutants, demonstrating that Fascin limits Myosin activity in nurse cells to promote migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C107 show that both Y-27632 treatment (migration index 1.1 vs 0.78) and germline MRLC knockdown (migration index 0.91 vs 0.65) rescue migration in fascin mutants (Figure 4). The cell-specific knockdown data (C105-C106) showing that germline MRLC knockdown reduces nurse cell but not border cell Myosin supports the conclusion that nurse cell Myosin is the critical target. The rescue is functionally significant and statistically supported.

results.result: Fascin's actin bundling activity is required to limit Myosin activation, as phosphomimetic Fascin (S52E) that cannot bundle actin fails to suppress increased Myosin in fascin mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 demonstrate that wild-type GFP-Fascin reduces active MRLC in fascin mutants while phosphomimetic S52E does not (Figure 5D-E). The partial rescue of migration by S52E (C114, migration index 0.90 vs 0.80) compared to full rescue by wild-type Fascin supports that bundling is required but also suggests additional Fascin functions contribute to migration (C115). The molecular mechanism is consistent with the model that bundled actin precludes Myosin binding.

results.result: Fascin acts in border cells to control Myosin activity and stiffness in both the border cells and their substrate nurse cells, revealing non-autonomous regulation of substrate stiffness by migrating cells.
results.evaluation: The cell-specific knockdown experiments (C118-C121, Figure 6) show that border cell Fascin knockdown increases Myosin on both border cells and nurse cells, while germline knockdown only affects nurse cells. AFM measurements (C123-C124, Figure 6H) confirm that both germline (1.5X) and border cell (1.8X) knockdown increase nurse cell stiffness. The rescue experiment (C126-C127, Figure 7) showing that somatic Fascin expression reduces both Myosin and nurse cell stiffness provides strong support. The Rok-CAT experiment (C129) demonstrates this is not Fascin-specific, strengthening the general principle.

results.result: Collectively migrating cells play a critical role in controlling the mechanical properties of their substrate to promote their own migration, shifting the paradigm from substrate-centric to bidirectional mechanical regulation.
results.evaluation: This paradigm-shifting conclusion (C9, C223) is supported by the convergence of all experimental results showing that border cells control nurse cell stiffness through Fascin-mediated Myosin regulation. The claim represents a synthesis of the major findings (C1-C8) and is well-supported by the data. However, the generalization to other contexts (C10) remains speculative as it is only demonstrated in the Drosophila border cell system.

results.result: AFM measurements reveal that fascin-null follicles have significantly increased nurse cell stiffness (25.9 kPa vs 10.1 kPa, >2-fold increase) while basement membrane stiffness remains unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present AFM data (Figure 3D) showing no change in basement membrane stiffness (0-100nm indentation: 24.2 vs 26.5 kPa, p>0.05) but significant increase in nurse cell stiffness (310-550nm indentation: 10.1 vs 25.9 kPa, p<0.0001). The use of two indentation ranges to separate tissue layers is methodologically sound and based on prior work (C90-C92). The >2-fold increase calculation (C95) is accurate and the conclusion (C96) is well-supported.

results.result: The force balance between border cells and nurse cells is not specific to Fascin, as directly increasing Myosin activity in border cells through constitutively active Rok phenocopies Fascin knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 shows that border cell expression of Rok-CAT increases active MRLC on both nurse cells and border cells (Figure 7—supplement 1, p<0.0001 and p<0.001), phenocopying Fascin knockdown. This demonstrates the principle is general to Myosin regulation rather than Fascin-specific (C137). The inference that border cells play a larger role in force balance (C172) is supported by the cell-specific experiments.

results.result: Live imaging reveals that Fascin limits Myosin dynamics on border cells, with fascin-null follicles showing significantly slower MRLC-GFP puncta dynamics (151.8s vs 70.2s lifetime).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 present live imaging data (Figure 2G-I, Videos 1-2) showing that MRLC-GFP puncta lifetime more than doubles in fascin mutants (p<0.0001). The conclusion (C82) that Fascin limits Myosin dynamics is well-supported. The observation is consistent with the increased Myosin activation seen in fixed samples and provides temporal resolution to the phenotype.

results.result: Active Myosin is enriched on nurse cell membranes surrounding the border cell cluster on all sides in both wild-type and fascin mutants, though the spatial distribution pattern differs between pMRLC staining and MRLC-GFP imaging.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 observes that active Myosin is enriched on all sides of the cluster in both genotypes (Figure 2A-B), and C67 notes no change in spatial distribution despite increased intensity. However, C140-C143 acknowledge differences between pMRLC and MRLC-GFP patterns and offer speculation (C141-C143) about technical reasons. The spatial distribution claim lacks quantitative analysis and the speculation about technical differences is not experimentally validated. More rigorous spatial analysis would be needed to fully support these claims.

results.result: Loss of Fascin does not affect F-actin levels (phalloidin intensity), nurse cell cytoplasmic pMRLC intensity, or Myosin heavy chain protein levels.
results.evaluation: These negative controls (Figure 2—supplement 1C-F) are important for demonstrating that the observed effects are specific to Myosin activation at membranes rather than changes in protein expression or F-actin levels. The Western blot data (C70) and fluorescence intensity measurements (C68-C69) show no significant differences, supporting the specificity of the Myosin activation phenotype.

results.result: The Fascin-Myosin regulatory mechanism is likely conserved in cancer metastasis, where phosphorylated Fascin may promote metastasis by allowing increased Myosin activation.
results.evaluation: While the manuscript provides extensive citations about Fascin and Myosin roles in cancer (C150-C156), the speculation about conservation (C10, C149) and the mechanism in cancer (C158, C160) is not directly tested. The supporting evidence from Hashimoto et al. 2007 (C159) about S39E Fascin promoting colon carcinoma migration is suggestive but not definitive. The apparent paradox (C157) that increased Fascin should reduce Myosin is addressed speculatively through phosphorylation, but this requires experimental validation in cancer systems.

results.result: Fascin has multiple non-bundling functions including microtubule regulation, nuclear functions, and LINC complex interactions that may contribute to border cell migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164 cite literature showing Fascin's diverse functions, and C161 infers from the partial S52E rescue that non-bundling functions contribute to migration. However, these alternative functions are not experimentally tested in this manuscript. The speculation about LINC complex involvement in border cell invasion (C165) is reasonable but untested. Claim C166 appropriately acknowledges this limitation.

results.result: Previous work suggested nurse cells exert force on border cells, but loss of Fascin in nurse cells may not cause severe enough changes to elicit border cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C169 accurately cite prior work (Aranjuez et al. 2016), but the speculation in C171 about why germline Fascin knockdown doesn't affect border cell Myosin is not experimentally tested. The observation (C170) that nurse cell shape doesn't change is qualitative. This represents an attempt to reconcile the current findings with prior work, but the mechanism remains unclear and would require additional experiments to resolve.

results.result: The spatial and temporal dynamics of how border cells regulate nurse cell stiffness remain unclear due to current technical limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C182 present the authors' interpretation that stiffening occurs on all sides based on imaging data, but C183 appropriately acknowledges that current methods lack sufficient resolution. The speculation about potential local stiffening (C173, C178) and the suggestion for future studies (C184) are reasonable. This represents an honest assessment of the study's limitations and appropriately identifies areas for future investigation.

results.result: The cellular connections mediating Myosin-dependent force transmission between border cells and nurse cells remain unclear, though E-Cadherin-based adhesions are candidates.
results.evaluation: Claim C185 identifies a knowledge gap, and C186-C187 cite prior work showing limited ECM and Integrin-independence. The speculation about E-Cadherin (C188) is supported by citations but not tested. Claim C189 appropriately identifies this as an area needing additional work. This represents an honest assessment of what is not known about the mechanism.

results.result: The mechanism by which increased Myosin activity impairs migration likely involves effects on delamination and protrusion dynamics through altered substrate stiffness and Rac polarization.
results.evaluation: This section (C192-C203) is largely speculative, connecting the current findings to prior observations about delamination and protrusion defects. While the speculation is well-reasoned and supported by citations (C197-C199, C201), the proposed mechanisms are not directly tested in this manuscript. The inference about Myosin cycling (C193) is reasonable but the detailed mechanistic proposals (C194-C196, C200-C202) require experimental validation.
